title: AusSuper frustrated with Link as death benefits mess escalated
full_text:
The board of AustralianSuper was unimpressed by a presentation Link’s chief executive and his deputy made to the industry fund, concluding its administrative provider did not accept the gravity of the delayed death benefits problem.
“There remained an apparent lack of alignment between the organisations and that Link did not have the requisite sense of urgency to address the fund’s concerns”, according to the minutes of the April 28 meeting which were documented in a statement of agreed facts tendered to the Federal Court as part of AusSuper and ASIC’s settlement.
Vivek Bhatia was the CEO of Link at the time, now called MUFG Pension & Market Services. The meeting was four months before AusSuper decided to hold a formal investigation into the matter, but it was not the first time Link had heard of its client’s dissatisfaction, as the matter was raised CEO to CEO in August 2022.
AusSuper then wrote to Mr Bhatia on 23 August 2023, stating: “Our auditors have got involved as to whether we have breached our obligation to pay it in ‘a reasonable time’.”
AustralianSuper could be forced to cough up as much as $30m in fines after conceding it did not pay out death benefits across thousands of cases quickly enough.
The corporate cop launched court proceedings against the nation’s biggest super fund last year, alleging it did not pay out death benefits sufficiently in more than 7000 cases over a five-year period to 2024.
ASIC in court documents cited some families having to wait for up to four years to receive death benefits for deceased relatives. In less severe cases, families still had to wait four months – found to be well beyond the “as soon as practicable” guide given by law.
It was also found that dead members had been charged account fees.
While AusSuper had already agreed to accept liability and pay a fine in Federal Court earlier this year, a Wednesday hearing saw judge David O’Callaghan call into question some of the facts of the submissions made, conceding it could impact the final penalty.
ASIC had previously held the fine should be of no less than $30m.
AusSuper rejected the claims before ASIC’s court proceedings were underway.
ASIC initially found that the board and executive level of the super fund were aware of issues as early as 2021, but did not do enough to fix them.
ASIC on Wednesday softened its stance on what level of penalty should apply given the top brass knew, after ASIC said AusSuper’s executives wrapped their collective minds properly around the issue the next year.
The proceedings also uncovered that the initial steps of bereaved family members receiving the materials on how to make their claim took far too long. Contracted out through Link Administration Services, the process which was agreed should take five days instead took 30 days at points in 2021, after Covid led to a ramp-up in claims which could not be dealt with quickly enough.
AusSuper CEO Paul Schroder received a complaint on 29 December 2022, which he forwarded to the quality manager, which told the fund: “there has been little to no communication regarding next steps from Australian Super and I have had to do all the follow up which is disengaging and unacceptable given that my sister and I are grieving the loss of a loved one,” according to an agreed statement of facts.
AusSuper no longer outsources its claims functions after Link could not keep up mid-pandemic.
“This should have [been] handled much better by the Links claims team and speaks to the poor service that members/people are experiencing on a regular basis,” wrote the senior manager for member advocacy to the chief member officer.
Cbus last year was ordered to pay $23.5m in fines, and seperately decided to pay $32m in compensation, for similar breaches, after a court found the super fund had inadequate oversight over its own third-party claims handling, resulting in more than 7000 members being forced to wait longer than necessary.
AusSuper was fined $27m in February last year after ASIC found it failed to merge duplicate member accounts, resulting in approximately $69m in lost funds for members due to duplicate administration fees and insurance premiums as well as the loss from potential compound earnings.
